Body size varies considerably within each sex: field records consistently show males ranging from 300 to 670 grams, and females from 300 to 450 grams, with the heaviest individuals generally encountered in higher-quality habitats on the mainland. This dimorphism is thought to be driven by male-male competition for access to females during the breeding season, as larger body size confers an advantage in agonistic encounters. The ultimate wet weight for females (450 grams) [Wwi = 450 grams] represents a plateau achieved after the completion of somatic growth, which in this species appears to occur well after sexual maturation. Comparative data from the closely related northern brown bandicoot (Isoodon macrourus) suggest that the mass at birth is quite small, with neonates weighing approximately 0.18 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.18 grams], a value that has been applied to I. auratus in the absence of species-specific measurements. Such altricial newborns are entirely dependent on maternal milk and undergo a protracted period of development within the pouch.

The gestation period of the golden bandicoot is remarkably brief, lasting only 12 days [tg = 12 days] when assessed at a maternal body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], one of the shortest gestation lengths documented among Australian marsupials.
